ann_116.original: Direct terms: the input edges that go straight to the output (the root keeps 0 direct edges of its own), gathered in identity_0 as one weighted sum of the z-scored inputs (the long linear formula is attached as analytical_formula evidence). This is the backbone of the model: switching the whole part off lowers the training AUC from 0.911 to 0.492. The largest single term is being married to a civilian spouse, a direct weight of -2.46 per sd of its indicator (towards high income); switching that one edge off lowers the AUC to 0.669. Other large direct weights: capital gains -2.01 per sd (capital_gain_thresholds adds more above a threshold), education level -0.65 per sd, divorced -0.69, male sex -0.34, hours per week -0.31, capital losses -0.27, other-service occupation 0.37 and Honduras 1.88 per sd (Honduras is described under capital_gain_thresholds). Prediction (self-probe): education level reaches the output through its own direct edge, so for the typical case the model's low-income probability falls steadily as the level rises: 92% at 1 on the 1-16 scale, 59% at 9 on the 1-16 scale and 20% at 16 on the 1-16 scale. In the whole model the typical case gets 75% as a woman and 59% as a man, and 71% at 20 hours a week against 47% at 60 hours. These directions (more education, being male, longer hours, marriage and capital income each lowering the predicted chance of low income) match the census income literature.
ann_116.proposed: Most inputs add up here one by one: more education, longer hours and capital gains and losses lower the predicted chance of a low income, and being never married, widowed or a woman (with the household role such people have in the data) raises it.

ann_117.original: Capital-gain thresholds. Capital gains are read by two hinges that open at nearly the same amount. Node 1594 opens between 4900 US dollars and 5000 US dollars, node 9424 between 5000 US dollars and 5100 US dollars (in the training data 0 rows with gains up to 5000 US dollars have 9424 on, and 0 rows above 5100 US dollars have it off). Above the threshold 9424 pushes the score towards high income, and 1594 drains node 1013, a standing push towards low income that the model gives almost everyone: 1013 is on for 38744 of 39073 training rows, and for the typical case (no gains) the part adds 4.28 to the score. For the typical (married) case that push is gone between 21500 US dollars and 22000 US dollars; never-married people start lower (1013 is 0.84 for them against 1.77 for the married typical case), so it empties earlier: 61 training rows with gains under 20000 US dollars have it at zero, and 61 of them are never married. Through this part, never-married rows get 1.97 on average against 3.82 for married-civilian-spouse rows. Prediction (self-probe): for the typical case the low-income probability falls slowly with gains through the direct edge, then faster once the hinges open: 59% at no gains, 30.4% at 4500 US dollars, 28.2% at 4900 US dollars, 20.5% at 5500 US dollars and 0.01% at 15000 US dollars; the model does this. The 1878 rows with 9424 on have an observed low-income rate of 5.8% and a mean prediction of 7.6%. Honduras also feeds 1013: for a Honduras-born typical case 1013 is 34.5 and the score 179, so the model is certain of low income; this regime is fitted to 14 training rows (observed rate 85.7%, mean prediction 100.0%). A small tail (1013 to 1172 to 9617, with Cambodia entering 1172) adds little: fixing 9617 at zero leaves the AUC at 0.9108. Switching the whole part off lowers the AUC from 0.9108 to 0.9016. In domain terms: a capital gain of a few thousand dollars is a strong sign of high income, and the model turns it into a near-certain high-income prediction.
ann_117.proposed: In this part, capital gains change nothing until about 4883 US dollars, then lower the predicted chance of a low income steadily (for a typical person from about 59% to about 36% at 6849 US dollars); never-married people get a smaller standing push towards a low income, and being born in Honduras gives above 99% from 14 training people.

ann_118.original: Youth gate. Node 251 adds a push towards low income for younger people, larger the younger they are, but it stays off for other-service workers. Prediction (self-probe): for the typical case (professional specialty) the node is 0.014 at 37 years and 0.000 at 38 years, so it switches off between those two ages, at about the median age; at 30 years it adds 0.81 to the score through this part and the whole-model low-income probability is 77%, against 59% at 38 years. Partner: with the occupation set to other service the node stays at zero at each probed age from 17 years to 62 years, and in the training data none of the 3916 other-service workers has it on (0 rows). The model does this. A consequence worth checking: at 17 years a professional gets 94% but an other-service worker 88%, because other-service workers miss the youth push (they carry their own direct term instead). In the data the gate is on for 17545 training rows (44.9%), adds 1.04 to their score on average through this part, and their observed low-income rate is 85.0%. Switching it off lowers the AUC from 0.9108 to 0.9046. In domain terms: younger workers earn less, and the model adds this on top of the linear age term.
ann_118.proposed: People younger than about 37 years, outside other-service work, get a push towards a low income that shrinks steadily with age; it acts on 17545 of 39073 training people and raises the typical such person's predicted chance from about 94% to about 98%.

ann_119.original: Marital switches. Node 3583 fires for never-married people and adds a push towards low income; node 8342 is on for every row (share 1.0), so it is a linear term in widowed that pushes widowed people towards high income. 3583 is on for 12914 rows: 0 of them are not never-married and 0 never-married rows have it off. Through this part never-married rows get 0.41 on average and widowed rows -2.05 (relative to the part's baseline, 8342 at its training mean). Prediction (self-probe): sweeping marital status for the typical case, 3583 is 1.38 for never married and 0.00 for divorced, and 8342 is 6.87 for widowed against 1.12 for divorced; the part contributes 0.41 (never married), -2.05 (widowed) and 0.06 (divorced). The model does this. In the whole model marital status also acts through the direct terms and capital_gain_thresholds: the typical case gets 59% married to a civilian spouse, 97% never married, 96% divorced and 94% widowed. Switching this part off lowers the AUC from 0.9108 to 0.9091.
ann_119.proposed: Being never married pushes the predicted chance of a low income up (to about 67% through this part) and being widowed pushes it down (to about 15%), for a typical person who is then not in a family.

Armed forces (node 6334): on for the 12 armed-forces rows (0 other rows); through this part it adds -79.7 to their score, so the model predicts 0.0% low-income probability for them, although 9 of the 12 have low income. Fitted to 12 rows and against their observed outcome. Tenth grade (node 7843): on for the 1156 tenth-grade rows (0 other rows), adding 0.42 towards low income. Self-employed, not incorporated, or born in Guatemala (node 574): on for 3103 rows (0 rows outside those two groups), adding 0.44 on average for the self-employed and 4.58 for the 72 Guatemala-born rows. ann_123.original: The model's score is the sum of four parts plus the output bias, passed through a sigmoid to give the predicted probability of low income (the dataset's at-most-50k class): the direct terms, the capital-gain thresholds, the youth gate and the category switches. The root has 0 direct input edges of its own, so each connected input acts through one of these parts. On the training split the AUC is 0.9108, the mean prediction 75.7% and the observed rate 76.1%. By ablation the direct terms carry most of the ranking (AUC 0.492 without them), then the capital-gain thresholds (0.9016), the youth gate (0.9046) and the category switches (0.9087). Prediction (self-probe): the typical case (a married man of 37 years in professional specialty, no capital gains) gets 59%; with 15000 US dollars of gains the model gives 0.01%, and as a never-married own child of 25 years it gives 99%. The model does this. Fitted regimes on tiny groups (Honduras, armed forces) give certain predictions and are described in their parts.
ann_123.proposed: The model adds four parts: most inputs count directly, capital gains above about 4883 US dollars push towards a higher income, younger people get a push towards a low income, and category switches add pushes for single groups; for a typical person the predicted chance of a low income is about 59%.

Prediction (self-probe): the typical case (a married man of 37 years in professional specialty, no capital gains) gets 59%; with 15000 US dollars of gains the model gives 0.01%, and as a never-married own child of 25 years it gives 99%. parts.name: direct_terms
parts.original_hypothesis: Direct terms: the input edges that go straight to the output (the root keeps 0 direct edges of its own), gathered in identity_0 as one weighted sum of the z-scored inputs (the long linear formula is attached as analytical_formula evidence). This is the backbone of the model: switching the whole part off lowers the training AUC from 0.911 to 0.492. The largest single term is being married to a civilian spouse, a direct weight of -2.46 per sd of its indicator (towards high income); switching that one edge off lowers the AUC to 0.669. Other large direct weights: capital gains -2.01 per sd (capital_gain_thresholds adds more above a threshold), education level -0.65 per sd, divorced -0.69, male sex -0.34, hours per week -0.31, capital losses -0.27, other-service occupation 0.37 and Honduras 1.88 per sd (Honduras is described under capital_gain_thresholds). Prediction (self-probe): education level reaches the output through its own direct edge, so for the typical case the model's low-income probability falls steadily as the level rises: 92% at 1 on the 1-16 scale, 59% at 9 on the 1-16 scale and 20% at 16 on the 1-16 scale. In the whole model the typical case gets 75% as a woman and 59% as a man, and 71% at 20 hours a week against 47% at 60 hours. These directions (more education, being male, longer hours, marriage and capital income each lowering the predicted chance of low income) match the census income literature.

parts.original_hypothesis: Capital-gain thresholds. Capital gains are read by two hinges that open at nearly the same amount. reference_patient.definition: the typical patient: the median training patient for every number and the most common training category for every category (not a real patient); an input the data ties to a category takes its typical value within that category (linked inputs)

confidence_rules.clearly: a meaningful change in predicted risk for a typical patient (at least 5% points), the test split agrees (same sign, and its bootstrap interval over test patients excludes no benefit), and every group has at least 20 training patients
confidence_rules.consistently across patients: the claim holds for at least 90% of training patients (range across patients); this is not a significance statement
confidence_rules.on the training data only: the test split disagrees (opposite sign, or no benefit on test patients) or is unclear (its interval includes no benefit), or no test check is available
confidence_rules.slightly: the change in predicted risk for a typical patient is below 5% points
confidence_rules.the model has little data on this: a compared group has fewer than 20 training patients
